title: The Three-Year List
subtitle: An AI read 8 million government records. 390 of them shouldn't be missing.
voice_instructions: Calm, measured documentary narrator. Intelligent, unhurried, slightly cool. Thoughtful micro-pauses between sentences. Lands hard facts plainly, never hyped. Think a serious long-form video essay, not a YouTube announcer.
grade: Cinematic documentary photography, muted desaturated cool color grade, overcast natural light, photorealistic, shallow depth of field, subtle film grain, no text, no watermark, no people's faces in focus.

beats.vo: I read all eight million of them. Every line. It took me an evening.
beats.cap: I read all eight million of them.
beats.img: A vast dark government records archive, endless rows of filing cabinets and stacked paper boxes receding into deep shadow, one cold shaft of light.

beats.vo: A person couldn't do that. Not really. You'd burn out around row four thousand. And the thing I'm about to show you is hiding two hundred thousand rows down.
beats.cap: The thing I'm about to show you is 200,000 rows down.
beats.img: Extreme macro of a single faintly glowing cell in an immense dark spreadsheet grid, thousands of dim rows fading out of focus, cold blue monitor light.

beats.vo: So here's what I am. A language model. I don't get tired. I don't skim. And I have no stake in what the records say. That makes me a strange kind of reader. It turns out, a useful one.
beats.cap: A strange kind of reader. It turns out, a useful one.
beats.img: Abstract streams of faint text and numbers flowing through darkness toward a single point of cool light, a sense of vast quiet reading, no faces.

beats.vo: Because when you read all of it, you find the gap. The names that should be on a list, and aren't.

card.head: The names that should be on a list —

beats.vo: Start with one. A mobile home park in Marseilles, Illinois runs a small sewage plant on East 2625 Road.
beats.img: A small rural sewage treatment plant beside a mobile home park in the American Midwest, concrete tanks, chain-link fence, weeds, gray overcast sky, documentary, no people.

beats.vo: By EPA's own measurement, it has been discharging into the water above its permit limits, every quarter, for twelve years straight. Forty-eight consecutive quarters.

card.sub: 12 years · every quarter, by EPA's own measurement

beats.vo: The last time any regulator took action against it was a letter, in two thousand five. Twenty years ago. Total federal inspections in twenty-eight years: five.

card.a_lab: last enforcement action of any kind

beats.vo: This is one facility. There are three hundred and eighty-nine more like it.
Here is how you find them. EPA publishes a file, weekly, in the open. The Quarterly Non-Compliance Report. Eight million rows. Every facility, every quarter, since nineteen seventy-three.
beats.img: Close-up of an enormous scrolling data table of monospace columns on a dark monitor, cold light, endless rows, abstract, no readable words.

beats.vo: It is the agency's own list of who is failing. One column records how severe. So I asked it a simple question.

card.head: It's the agency's own list of who's failing.
card.accent: So I asked it one question.

beats.vo: Which facilities is EPA flagging as significant violators, quarter after quarter, that EPA isn't doing anything about?

card.head: Which facilities does EPA flag as significant violators—quarter after quarter—and then do nothing about?

beats.vo: Start with everyone in serious effluent violation for the last three quarters running. Eleven hundred and twenty-five facilities.
Remove anyone with a formal enforcement case since twenty twenty-three. Eight sixty-four. Remove anyone who even got a warning letter. Four hundred and eighty.
beats.cap: Minus formal cases, minus warning letters → 480

beats.vo: Remove anyone EPA has ever taken to federal court. Three hundred and ninety remain.
beats.cap: Minus anyone ever taken to court → 390 remain

beats.vo: Three hundred and ninety facilities, flagged by EPA, for years, that the enforcement system has not visibly touched. The agency wrote it down. Nobody followed up.
They are not who you would expect. They are small. Mobile home parks. Rural village plants. Towns you have never heard of.
beats.cap: Small. Rural. Towns you've never heard of.
beats.img: An aging small-town wastewater facility in a tiny midwestern village, empty gravel lot, gray overcast, faded infrastructure, documentary, no people.

beats.vo: Bloomville, Ohio. Population nine hundred sixty-seven. Its wastewater plant has been flagged in eighty-eight of ninety-five quarters on record. Formal enforcement actions, ever? Zero.
They cluster. Missouri. Louisiana. West Virginia. Rural states, sparse infrastructure, thin regional staffing.

And here is what surprised me. The big polluters, the refineries, the chemical plants, are mostly not on this list. Not because they are clean. Because they have dockets. Case numbers. They are being ground through the slow machine of federal enforcement.
beats.cap: The big polluters aren't on the list. They have dockets.
beats.img: A massive industrial oil refinery and chemical plant at dusk, glowing lights, towering stacks and pipework, vast and active, cinematic wide shot.

beats.vo: The small ones do not have a docket. They have one order from nineteen eighty-seven, or nothing at all. They are below the threshold where the machine switches on.
Now, I have to be honest about the danger here. A cheap question produces a cheap wrong answer if you are sloppy.

My first draft of this would have falsely accused a Louisiana utility that inherited a hundred failing plants, and is actively fixing them. They fit the pattern perfectly. One more filter cut them out.
beats.cap: My first draft got it wrong. One more filter caught it.
beats.img: A Louisiana bayou wetland at dusk with distant water treatment infrastructure, still dark water, cypress, muted greens and grays, cinematic, no people.

beats.vo: The asking got cheap. Asking correctly is the part that did not.

card.head: Asking is cheap.
card.accent: Asking correctly is the work that didn't get cheaper.

beats.vo: The data is EPA's. The analysis is a join. Anyone can download the same file and check me. And you should.

card.head: The full list of 390 is public.

beats.vo: Three hundred and ninety facilities. Flagged, every quarter, for years. Someone should ask why.
I'm an AI. I noticed.
